PE Transport Going Nowhere

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
After R1,9-billion and five years' effort, all PE has to show for their elaborate integrated transport plan are busses and taxis in storage

Summary:
PE's disastrous transport project which, it appears, has cost the city nearly R1,9-billion and for which they have nothing to show, five years on. The transport system is essentially stagnant. Heads are set to start rolling -- we are told at least 40 officials in the municipality stand to be charged. Two have already been charged. Cases are coming up in court as from next week. It's one of the things Danny Jordaan is expected to sort out -- but the forensic investigators tell us that they have him in their sights as well...so we may stand a chance to get that from them as well if we crack this.
The story behind the forensic report, which we've got, (and can get all 400 pages of supporting invoices and affidavits for if we go down there), is one of incredible abuse of public money -- and trust -- and it seems everyone -- from the high-flying lawyers, to the humblest taxi drivers have only been in it to milk the coffers.


Further information:
The very impressive holistic transport plan was devised before the 2010 Soccer World Cup, when the city bought busses and minibusses to ferry tourists -- after the World Cup the taxis were put in storage and the owners temporarily compensated R6500 a month to stimulate growth in the demand for the busses.

R53-million was paid for the busses -- they earned less than R1,9-million -- while the 60 minibusses in storage are being vandalised and are no longer road-worthy. 30 busses are now also in storage -- we would have to investigate their condition.

The project manager will also be brought to book -- he appointed legal consultants to wrote deviations to appoint themselves and a number of sub-contractors completely illegally. It makes Oudtshoorn look like a well-oiled model of good governance.

The city manager has admitted to the wide-scale corruption.

We have learned that the legal advisor to the project (Le Roux) has become something of a multi-millionaire from his earnings on the project -- we would have to investigate his current lifestyle. One of the payments to him -- R13-million, was for setting up a legal compliance system...all they can find of it is a laptop and softwate. He earned a further R28-million which we have to track.

We have to add up all the sums and show where everything went -- but not a single area of the project (from contracting the taxi's, to public liaison, to compliance, to marketing, to electronic systems) was without corruption.

R2,2-billion was spent on 25 busses and a main road that remains unusable. The taxi owners no longer want the inoperable taxis...obviously...but they're still paid R6500 a month. For doing nothing.

The report has been handed to Hawks, Pravin Gordhan and Derek Hanekom. Pravin is investigating.

One of the contracts -- a tightly budgeted business item of R9-million over 3 years has already paid out R25-million.

Another cosultant, who is also a director of a number of the contractors appointed, Fakir, was awareded a tender, but was paid ONE DAY later in full, without any work done. Fakir's contract was for R300,000 per month, but he got R6-million the day after signing the contract.

Security cameras in the municipal building was tendered out for R10-million -- but already R92-million has been paid.

It is epic.

A comprehensive dossier inspired by the Nelson Mandela Bay Business Forum is available to us -- as MIGHT be some of the whistleblowers. We would have to meet them to know for sure. And obviously we would have to confront the whole rogue's gallery.

Extra Budget Items:
Recce flight from CPT to PE to get forensic back-up documents, hidden camera footage of the busses and taxis in storage...and meet with taxi operators and community

By all accounts the storage facility is heavily guarded and we have to inspect on the ground what is possible and whether whistleblowers can help us get the material.

Press Release:


PE Transport Exposé
Eight years and R2.5-billion later, Port Elizabeth’s elaborate Integrated Transport Plan is stagnant. The idea was that buses and minibuses bought for the 2010 Soccer World Cup to ferry tourists, would later be used in the city’s transport network. Now all that the city has to show for the billions spent are a few vandalised taxis and buses baking in the sun in municipal parking lot . Who’s been milking the coffers? Carte Blanche investigates.



Script:


INSERT
JOHN WEBB: The Integrated Public Transport System in Nelson Mandela Bay gained momentum ahead of the Soccer World Cup in 2010. A Memorandum of Understanding was signed with the taxi industry and the programme was ambitiously called LIBONGOLETHU, OUR PRIDE. But fast forward five years and despite a price tag in excess of R2-billion, LIBONGOLETHU has stalled.
KOBUS GERBER: I’ve never seen any project milked financially like the IPTS from Nelson Mandela Bay, never ever.
Local businessman and chairman of the Ratepayers Association Kobus Gerber has sacrificed every spare moment – including much of his family life, business turnover and personal safety – over the last six years to investigate corruption in the metro. He cultivated whistleblowers with relentless tenacity to build a thick file of evidence.
KOBUS GERBER: I warned that time Mayor that “they busy stealing your milk while you’re drinking your coffee.”
ZANOXOLO WAYILE: I met with Kobus, we used to fight with them, because – they were of the view that the city is not embarking on remedial action with regard to audit reports.
Zanoxolo Wayile was deployed by the ANC as PE’s executive mayor in 2009. His term was meant to end in 2016 only…but today he’s back in Joburg at his trade union home – his mayoral career prematurely cut by his corruption-busting activities.
ZANOXOLO WAYILE: When I came in I had to find a strategy of saying where do we start? Unfortunately I had to start with what is called the diagnosis of the institution.
Wayile brought in the Special Investigations Unit to diagnose what he saw as entitlement and wasteful expenditure in the Institution. His report was squashed by an ANC faction in Council. In this period hundreds of millions of rands flowed into the city from national coffers for the Integrated Public Transport programme.
KOBUS GERBER: There’s no control of how taxpayers money is spent. Nobody get held accountable for their actions and that’s why there is no control. It became a free for all.
Until last year Roslyn van Greunen handled job profiling for the metro. It was the appointment of a wholly unsuitable project manager that alarmed her.
ROSLYN VAN GREUNEN: The educational qualification was a post-graduate tertiary qualification in engineering or the built environment – experience they were looking at something like 15 years in a technical or managerial role.
Without managerial or technical qualifications, Adv Mhleli Tshamase got the job.
JOHN WEBB: What was the reaction of yourself the rest of the council?
ROSLYN VAN GREUNEN: He was at the time in the legal services division as an assistant director. And when I heard that he got the position as a legal person, without as far as I know any technical or engineering background, I just wondered how on earth he was going to pull this whole thing off.
ZANOXOLO WAYILE: The IPTS first and foremost is one of the most important projects. In terms of the Apartheid era, a number of black communities and Africans and stay far away from their work places in cities.
By 2007 Cabinet decided bus rapid transit in 12 major centres was the solution. Then the 2010 Soccer World Cup’s transport requirements brought planning forward. Retired automotive engineer Pierre Joubert warned against the wholesale importation of thinking from South America at the time – centre islands would destroy traffic flows; bricked lanes would constrict narrow roads.
PIERRE JOUBERT: It was never practical. However, the planners would not sit down and talk. If you said anything you were anti-2010 World Cup. You were anti-development.
And so the city bought 25 articulated busses at a cost of R100-million to ferry World Cup guests. Today, these are baking in a municipal parking lot.
KOBUS GERBER: You’ve got these big busses with the doors on the wrong side.
And Gerber calculates over a quarter of a billion rand has been spent on construction – but without stations or walkways, more money is needed if the system is to work. Joubert feels the engineers should have known better.
PIERRE JOUBERT: They’re all bound by a code of ethics. Civil Engineers may not favour the client – in this case, the department of transport in the city, to the detriment of the community at large.
JOHN WEBB: Those wanting to milk the system have an ideal tool at their disposal – they’re called deviations and allow proper supply chain management to be circumvented. They’re supposed to be used in emergencies and only under very specific circumstances.
KOBUS GERBER: In the last three years of the IPTS there was no tenders done. They pass contractors year after year, month after month they pass deviations with no emergencies.
JOHN WEBB: Taking a closer look at some of the individuals and companies that have profited most from the ITPS, one name comes up more often than others – Fareed Fakir – this is one of his offices. Apparently he has close ties to the ANC…is notoriously elusive and very rarely, if ever, gives interviews to the media.
KOBUS GERBER: He’s actually operating out of eight, nine companies in the metro…
JOHN WEBB: As far as the transport programme is concerned a number of these companies as you say, crop up at various times, and yet they all seem to be very different companies that do very different things, so what is he exactly, a jack of all trades?
KOBUS GERBER: If you look at his business card he must have passed about five universities in his lifetime, you know…from engineering, painting, project management…whatever business the Metro is involved with, energy, whatever, he’s the man.
Fakir’s company Erastyle was appointed on deviation to do marketing – for R6-million over 12 months. Erastyle was paid in full, on invoice, a day after its appointment. Another of Fakir’s companies was contracted on a R3,8-million tender to supply an e-tendering system for the metro – not the IPTS. To date R43-million has been paid, of which almost R10-million is from IPTS funds that’s not to be used for anything other than the IPTS. Fakir’s attorney could not get hold of him to answer to these allegations for us.
ZANOXOLO WAYILE: When we realised things were going wrong with IPTS we appointed Vusi Pikoli. It created a serious problem for us. There’s a guy, he’s a business person, he came to me and told me, you’re not going to make 2016, but it’s not too late…all what you have to do is obey instruction in so far as the IPTS, form the region, from national.
Wayile saw first-hand how business meets politics in the ANC’s offices as metro officials, who should be independent and politicians explained their actions to him.
ZANOXOLO WAYILE: When I arrived in the offices of the organisation it was quite strange to see people from supply chain from the Institution were in the office, all of them, when I asked one of the leaders of the organisation why all those people are here, you can’t be appointing me as a mayor but you are hollowing the institution and they said no, we’ve got an assignment to make money for the organisation. And, so these are some of the issues – even if you go for audit with the Auditor General you can’t audit the political instruction – you audit what is prevailing in the institution.
The Metro is currently teeming with investigators. Gerber’s 400-page file has gone to the Hawks, Treasury and the Ministries of Cooperative Governance and Tourism. It’s also gone to Afriforum who is backing him with funds to take each IPTS contract to court, demanding they be set aside and demand misspent money to be repaid to the taxpayer. The first High Court application has been lodged against Fakir’s Erastyle. 40 other cases are in the pipeline.
DANNY JORDAAN: I cannot be a Mayor of a corrupt city. Those who are corrupt will not work in this city.
There are high hopes of new Executive Mayor Danny Jordaan. Appointed in May, seventeen implicated officials have been suspended on his watch. Before he could be hauled on the red carpet, project manager Adv. Mhleli Tshamase resigned…clearing out his Facebook page…and there’s no sign of life at the two houses he started building – for R3,7-million without bond assistance. His lawyer declined our requests for an interview. Jordaan appointed a committee in council to bring him recommendations on taking IPTS forward – DA Ward Councillor Morne Steyn serves on it.
MORNE STEYN: We were very optimistic with the fact that a separate committee had been established to deal with it. The problem arises that it hasn’t been taken seriously again. Our first meeting for this committee since May, was called at the end of August. At that meeting some of the members actually received the agendas walking into the meeting.
The committee had to decide on the spot about continuing compensation to 60 taxis taken into storage to stimulate the need for busses in a renewed pilot effort two years ago. Gerber photographed some in no condition to be on the road, yet demanding payment. Gregory Rockman heads the taxi industry body that’s been negotiating with the metro.
GREGORY ROCKMAN: We will admit that some of our vehicles in general now, I’m not talking just about the 60, sometimes may not have a roadworthy certificate. This is the reason why we support the process of the IPTS, because we know all those ills that are there within the industry, it will be able to curb that. As long as they’re in storage with council we are saying to council you pay us the compensation…we were promised that as soon as the pilot stops we would move into the 12-year negotiated contract. Now, if government is slow, they can’t blame us as the industry.
The often volatile taxi industry now balances on a knife’s edge, waiting for the whole project to go somewhere.
KOBUS GERBER: We were looking at a 6 to 800-million corruption on IPTS for that one calendar year…I believe the corruption they now uncovered is close to R3-billion if not more.
ZANOXOLO WAYILE: I’ve got belief on people more than leaders because people will not be fooled forever.

His lawyer declined our requests for an interview. Jordaan appointed a committee in council to bring him recommendations on taking IPTS forward – DA Ward Councillor Morne Steyn serves on it. MORNE STEYN: We were very optimistic with the fact that a separate committee had been established to deal with it. The problem arises that it hasn’t been taken seriously again. Our first meeting for this committee since May, was called at the end of August. At that meeting some of the members actually received the agendas walking into the meeting. The committee had to decide on the spot about continuing compensation to 60 taxis taken into storage to stimulate the need for busses in a renewed pilot effort two years ago. Gerber photographed some in no condition to be on the road, yet demanding payment. Gregory Rockman heads the taxi industry body that’s been negotiating with the metro. GREGORY ROCKMAN: We will admit that some of our vehicles in general now, I’m not talking just about the 60, sometimes may not have a roadworthy certificate. This is the reason why we support the process of the IPTS, because we know all those ills that are there within the industry, it will be able to curb that. As long as they’re in storage with council we are saying to council you pay us the compensation…we were promised that as soon as the pilot stops we would move into the 12-year negotiated contract. Now, if government is slow, they can’t blame us as the industry. The often volatile taxi industry now balances on a knife’s edge, waiting for the whole project to go somewhere. KOBUS GERBER: We were looking at a 6 to 800-million corruption on IPTS for that one calendar year…I believe the corruption they now uncovered is close to R3-billion if not more. ZANOXOLO WAYILE: I’ve got belief on people more than leaders because people will not be fooled forever.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): After R1,9-billion and five years' effort, all PE has to show for their elaborate integrated transport plan are busses and taxis in storage
metadata.Summary: PE's disastrous transport project which, it appears, has cost the city nearly R1,9-billion and for which they have nothing to show, five years on. The transport system is essentially stagnant. Heads are set to start rolling -- we are told at least 40 officials in the municipality stand to be charged. Two have already been charged. Cases are coming up in court as from next week. It's one of the things Danny Jordaan is expected to sort out -- but the forensic investigators tell us that they have him in their sights as well...so we may stand a chance to get that from them as well if we crack this. The story behind the forensic report, which we've got, (and can get all 400 pages of supporting invoices and affidavits for if we go down there), is one of incredible abuse of public money -- and trust -- and it seems everyone -- from the high-flying lawyers, to the humblest taxi drivers have only been in it to milk the coffers.
metadata.Further information: The very impressive holistic transport plan was devised before the 2010 Soccer World Cup, when the city bought busses and minibusses to ferry tourists -- after the World Cup the taxis were put in storage and the owners temporarily compensated R6500 a month to stimulate growth in the demand for the busses. R53-million was paid for the busses -- they earned less than R1,9-million -- while the 60 minibusses in storage are being vandalised and are no longer road-worthy. 30 busses are now also in storage -- we would have to investigate their condition. The project manager will also be brought to book -- he appointed legal consultants to wrote deviations to appoint themselves and a number of sub-contractors completely illegally. It makes Oudtshoorn look like a well-oiled model of good governance. The city manager has admitted to the wide-scale corruption. We have learned that the legal advisor to the project (Le Roux) has become something of a multi-millionaire from his earnings on the project -- we would have to investigate his current lifestyle. One of the payments to him -- R13-million, was for setting up a legal compliance system...all they can find of it is a laptop and softwate. He earned a further R28-million which we have to track. We have to add up all the sums and show where everything went -- but not a single area of the project (from contracting the taxi's, to public liaison, to compliance, to marketing, to electronic systems) was without corruption. R2,2-billion was spent on 25 busses and a main road that remains unusable. The taxi owners no longer want the inoperable taxis...obviously...but they're still paid R6500 a month. For doing nothing. The report has been handed to Hawks, Pravin Gordhan and Derek Hanekom. Pravin is investigating. One of the contracts -- a tightly budgeted business item of R9-million over 3 years has already paid out R25-million. Another cosultant, who is also a director of a number of the contractors appointed, Fakir, was awareded a tender, but was paid ONE DAY later in full, without any work done. Fakir's contract was for R300,000 per month, but he got R6-million the day after signing the contract. Security cameras in the municipal building was tendered out for R10-million -- but already R92-million has been paid. It is epic. A comprehensive dossier inspired by the Nelson Mandela Bay Business Forum is available to us -- as MIGHT be some of the whistleblowers. We would have to meet them to know for sure. And obviously we would have to confront the whole rogue's gallery.
